title: Championing the Beautiful Struggle
author: Micah Chua
source: Wise AI for Educators (paulmatthews.substack.com), guest essay, November 8, 2026
summary: This guest essay by Micah Chua, shared by Paul Matthews in his Wise AI for Educators newsletter, offers teachers a way to talk with students about AI. Chua describes the tangled path of producing an essay, with all its ideating, drafting and blundering, and contrasts it with the smooth, frictionless path AI offers. He argues that students sense that outsourcing every hard task would end badly, costing them skills, wisdom and formation. His reframe is that the messy slog is what he calls the good stuff, and that struggle is itself the point of being at school, summed up in the phrase strength through the struggle. He says teachers should welcome scrappy drafts as evidence of thinking over polished but empty products, and that championing process makes AI misuse less attractive to students. Matthews closes with questions about where the good stuff happens in a classroom, how teachers respond to unpolished drafts, and whether AI can be used in ways that protect the good stuff.
points: Chua contrasts the tangled path of real work with AI's frictionless path, and argues students intuitively know outsourcing everything would cost them skills, wisdom and formation.
The reframe is that struggle is the good stuff of school, not an obstacle to it, summarised as strength through the struggle.
Teachers can signal what they value by welcoming scrappy, unpolished drafts that show a student's thinking rather than rewarding only the polished product.
Shifting the classroom narrative from final product to process makes AI misuse make less sense to students.
Matthews adds reflective questions on whether assessments reward the good stuff and whether AI can be used without removing it.
quotes: But I am convinced that within all learners, there is a subtle, lingering understanding that if we were to outsource every difficult task to AI, things would not end well. There would be no skill acquisition, no gaining of wisdom, and no formation.
To put a finer point on it, opting for the frictionless path has a student losing out on becoming the best version of themselves.
Struggle doesn’t get in the way of the good stuff. The struggle is the good stuff.

I love receiving scrappy, unpolished essays that may be far from perfect, but bear the evidence of a student wading in the depths of their thoughts, trying to untangle their ideas while reaching for the right words to express them.

The championing of struggle is a different narrative to the popular one that emphasises final product above all else, but it’s one that takes a keen interest in a student’s formation, not just what they produce.
When we shift the narrative to champion process (and the difficulties that come with that), then AI misuse makes less and less sense to a student.

AI remains an incredibly useful tool, but we must use it wisely. I use this image to give shape to what that wisdom might look like, because above all, it cannot take away from the beautiful struggle that is so crucial to the formation of our students.
